terms.definition: Serving variants to randomized user cohorts at the same time to measure which performs better on a business metric, whereas canaries compare health.
GitHub's Kubernetes operator that autoscales ephemeral self-hosted runners as Pods using runner scale sets.
Code in the API server request path, after authentication and authorization, that can mutate or reject objects before they are persisted, either built in or via webhooks and CEL policies.
An external HTTPS service the API server calls during admission, configured by a Mutating- or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration with failurePolicy, timeouts and match rules.
The Prometheus component that deduplicates, groups, silences and routes alerts to receivers such as email, chat or paging tools.
Red Hat's agentless automation tool that applies YAML playbooks of idempotent modules over SSH or WinRM.
A Linux security module that confines a program to a profile of allowed file, capability and network access, applied per container through securityContext.appArmorProfile.
A CNCF graduated GitOps controller and web UI that syncs Applications from Git, Helm or OCI sources into clusters, with ApplicationSets for fleet generation.
An Argo controller and Rollout CRD that add blue-green and canary strategies with metric analysis and traffic shaping on Kubernetes.
A project-scoped endpoint and credential (Azure Resource Manager with workload identity federation, Kubernetes, Docker registry, GitHub) that pipelines use to reach external systems.
The machine that runs Azure Pipelines jobs: Microsoft-hosted, self-hosted, VM scale set agents or Managed DevOps Pools.
Reusable YAML for stages, jobs, steps or variables; include templates insert content, while extends templates enforce an approved pipeline structure.
A library set of shared pipeline variables, optionally linked to Azure Key Vault secrets, reused across pipelines.
Azure Repos branch rules requiring minimum reviewers, linked work items, comment resolution, build validation, status checks and allowed merge types.
A CNCF incubating, open-source framework for developer portals, providing a software catalog, scaffolder templates, TechDocs and a plugin ecosystem.
A written incident review that records timeline, impact, contributing factors and tracked actions, focused on systems and processes rather than individual blame.
Running two production environments and switching all traffic from the current (blue) to the new (green) in one step, keeping blue ready for instant rollback.
Per-branch GitHub settings requiring reviews, status checks, signed commits or linear history before merging.
The versioned, immutable output of a build (package, image, binary, IaC bundle), promoted unchanged through environments.
Docker's default build engine (usable through buildx or buildctl) with parallel stages, cache import/export, secret and SSH mounts, and multi-platform builds.
An SLO-based alert that fires when the error budget is being consumed faster than sustainable, checked over long and short windows to balance speed and noise.
Date-based version numbers (for example 2026.10.1) that signal release time rather than compatibility.
Shifting a small, growing percentage of traffic to a new version while comparing its health metrics with the baseline, and aborting automatically on regression.
Forecasting demand and provisioning headroom so services meet their SLOs at peak at acceptable cost.
The non-Turing-complete expression language Kubernetes embeds in CRD validation rules, Validating and Mutating Admission Policies, authorization match conditions and DRA device selectors.
A CNCF-graduated controller that issues and renews X.509 certificates from ACME (Let's Encrypt), private CAs or cloud CAs for Ingress, Gateway and workload TLS.
A Linux kernel mechanism that limits and accounts for the CPU, memory and I/O of groups of processes, which is how container resource limits are enforced.
An open-source (Palo Alto Networks Prisma Cloud) static analysis scanner for misconfigurations in Terraform, CloudFormation, Bicep/ARM, Kubernetes, Helm and Dockerfiles.
An automated, versioned workflow of stages that builds, tests, packages and releases a change from commit to production.

A pipeline presenting a short-lived OIDC token from its CI platform to a cloud identity provider, which checks issuer, audience and subject claims before issuing temporary credentials, so no stored cloud secrets are needed.
A CNCF-graduated eBPF-based CNI offering kube-proxy replacement, L3-L7 policy, transparent WireGuard or IPsec encryption, a sidecarless mesh and Hubble observability.
Center for Internet Security hardening recommendations for control-plane, etcd, node and policy configuration, commonly checked with kube-bench.
The control-plane component that embeds cloud-specific control loops for nodes, routes and LoadBalancer Services, decoupling providers from core Kubernetes.
Per the CNCF, building and running scalable applications in dynamic environments using containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure and declarative APIs.
A CNCF-graduated specification and toolchain (pack, kpack) that builds OCI images from source without a Dockerfile, with rebasable run-image layers.
A Kubernetes SIG Cluster Lifecycle project that creates, upgrades and operates clusters declaratively through Kubernetes-style APIs and infrastructure providers.
A component that adds or removes nodes in predefined node groups when Pods are unschedulable or nodes are underused.

The SIG Network Policy API's cluster-scoped, priority-ordered policy, successor to AdminNetworkPolicy and BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy. Admin-tier rules are evaluated before namespaced NetworkPolicies, and Baseline-tier rules act as defaults after them, in CNIs that support it.
A cluster-scoped object (GA in v1.37) that publishes CA trust anchors, which Pods mount through projected volumes.
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation, the Linux Foundation project that hosts Kubernetes and other cloud native projects and, with the Linux Foundation, runs the Kubernetes certifications.
The Sandbox, Incubating and Graduated stages through which the CNCF Technical Oversight Committee advances projects based on adoption, governance and security criteria.
The share of lines, branches or paths that tests execute; a pipeline signal of how much tests reach, not proof of correctness.
GitHub's alerting and triage feature that ingests SARIF from CodeQL or third-party analyzers and surfaces alerts on pull requests and the Security tab.
A file mapping paths to the users or teams automatically requested for review, optionally required through branch protection or rulesets.

GitHub's semantic code analysis engine, which models code as a queryable database to find vulnerabilities through data-flow queries; it runs in code scanning through default setup (GitHub-managed) or advanced setup (a workflow you own), or through the CodeQL CLI in other CI.
A named set of CodeQL queries (default, security-extended, security-and-quality) or custom query and model packs that determines what a scan looks for.
An action defined in action.yml that bundles several steps to run inside the calling job, unlike JavaScript or Docker actions that run code.
An API object holding non-confidential key-value configuration that Pods consume as environment variables, command arguments or mounted files.
Divergence between infrastructure's declared configuration and its actual state, usually from manual or out-of-band changes, detected by plan/refresh, drift detection or GitOps reconciliation.
Keeping software and OS settings on existing machines in a desired state with idempotent tools (Ansible, PowerShell DSC, Chef, Puppet), as opposed to provisioning infrastructure.
An OPA-project CLI that tests structured configuration (Terraform plan JSON, Kubernetes YAML, Dockerfiles) against Rego policies, typically in CI.
A running, isolated process tree started from an image, confined by Linux namespaces and cgroups (or Windows isolation), sharing the host kernel unless sandboxed.
An immutable, layered filesystem bundle plus configuration metadata (entrypoint, environment, user) that a container runtime unpacks to start containers.
Matching the packages and files in an image's layers against vulnerability data (CVE feeds, VEX) with tools such as Trivy or Grype, in CI, registries and admission.
Attaching cryptographic signatures to image digests (for example with Sigstore cosign or Notation) so admission controllers can verify publisher and integrity before a workload runs.
A specification and plugin model that attaches Pods to the network and assigns their IPs, implemented by plugins such as Cilium, Calico, Azure CNI or Amazon VPC CNI.
Automated placement, scaling, networking, self-healing and rollout of containers across a cluster of machines.
A service implementing the OCI distribution API that stores and serves images and other OCI artifacts by repository, tag and digest.
Software that pulls images and runs containers; high-level runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O manage images and lifecycle and delegate process creation to a low-level OCI runtime such as runc.
The gRPC API the kubelet uses to ask a container runtime such as containerd or CRI-O to manage pod sandboxes, containers and images.
The gRPC specification that lets storage vendors ship out-of-tree drivers to provision, attach, mount, snapshot and expand volumes.
A CNCF-graduated container runtime daemon that manages image pull and storage, snapshots and container lifecycle, exposes the CRI to the kubelet and delegates to runc.
Keeping every change in a deployable state through automated pipelines, so releasing to production is a low-risk business decision that can happen at any time.
Automatically releasing every change that passes the pipeline to production, with no manual approval step.
The practice of merging small changes to a shared mainline frequently, with every change automatically built and tested.
Always-on, low-overhead sampling of CPU and memory use by code location in production; the emerging fourth signal, via OpenTelemetry profiles.
A commit-message convention (feat:, fix:, BREAKING CHANGE) from which tools derive semantic versions and changelogs.
An IDE chat mode in which Copilot plans and performs multi-file edits, runs terminal commands and tools (including MCP servers) and iterates on errors locally, with user approval.
AI-generated fix suggestions for code scanning alerts, offered in pull requests and for existing alerts, and used in security campaigns.
GitHub's terminal agent that answers questions, edits files, runs commands and uses MCP tools in interactive or scripted sessions.

An asynchronous Copilot agent that researches, plans and implements a task on one branch in an ephemeral cloud development environment (customised with copilot-setup-steps.yml, 59-minute session limit) and opens a pull request for review.
AI pull-request review that leaves comments and suggested changes, governed by policy and custom review instructions.

Repository, organization or enterprise settings (Business and Enterprise plans) that stop Copilot from using specified files or paths as context; exclusions are not honoured in VS Code Edit and Agent modes and do not cover symlinks or remote filesystems.

Standing instructions that Copilot applies automatically: repository-wide .github/copilot-instructions.md, path-specific .github/instructions/*.instructions.md with applyTo, and personal and organization instructions.
Enterprise and organization settings that enable or restrict Copilot features, models, MCP, code review and public-code matching for seat holders, with changes recorded in audit logs.
A reusable, checked-in task prompt (.github/prompts/*.prompt.md) invoked on demand in Copilot Chat, unlike always-applied custom instructions.
The policy that either blocks Copilot suggestions matching public GitHub code or allows them with code referencing and licence information.
Curated, shareable collections of repositories, files, issues and notes that ground Copilot answers for a task or team.
The CNCF-graduated, plugin-based DNS server that serves Kubernetes Service and Pod DNS records.
The waiting state of a container the kubelet keeps restarting after repeated failures, with exponentially growing delays (capped at five minutes by default).
A CNCF-graduated, Kubernetes-only CRI implementation that runs OCI containers through runc or crun and is versioned in lockstep with Kubernetes minor releases.
A controller that creates Jobs on a cron schedule, with time zone, concurrency policy, starting deadline and history limits.
A CNCF graduated Kubernetes extension that provisions and composes cloud infrastructure through CRDs and controllers, letting platform teams publish their own infrastructure APIs.
An API extension that registers a new resource type with an OpenAPI schema so the API server stores and serves custom objects.
A regular-expression pattern defined at repository, organization or enterprise level so that secret scanning finds organization-specific credentials.
The elapsed time from starting work on an item to finishing it; a flow metric distinct from DORA's change lead time (commit to production).
A controller that runs one copy of a Pod on every eligible node, typically for node agents such as log shippers, CNI or monitoring.
Evolving a schema either by ordered, versioned scripts (EF Core, Flyway, DbUp, Alembic) or by diffing a desired-state model (DACPAC with SqlPackage).
Describing the desired end state and letting a tool compute and apply the changes, rather than scripting imperative steps.

GitHub's dependency tooling: Dependabot alerts flag known-vulnerable dependencies from the dependency graph, security updates open PRs that fix them, and version updates open PRs that keep dependencies current.
GitHub-preset and custom rules that automatically dismiss or snooze Dependabot alerts matching criteria such as severity, package, ecosystem or dependency scope.
GitHub's inventory of a repository's direct and transitive dependencies, built from manifests, lock files and the dependency submission API and exportable as an SPDX SBOM.
A pull-request check that shows dependency changes and can block merges that add vulnerable or disallowed-license packages.
A named deployment target in GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines that carries protection rules or checks (approvals, wait timers, branch restrictions), scoped secrets and deployment history.
A container-based development environment defined by devcontainer.json (image or Dockerfile, features, extensions, ports), used by Codespaces and local IDEs.
The user interface of a platform (for example Backstage) for discovering services, docs and self-service actions; one surface of an internal developer platform, not the platform itself.
A kubelet plugin framework that advertises node hardware such as GPUs as countable extended resources.
A culture and set of practices that unite development and operations to deliver change quickly and safely through automation, shared ownership, fast feedback and continuous improvement.
Recording each request as a tree of timed spans across services, linked by propagated context, to locate latency and errors in distributed systems.
A base image containing only the application runtime and its libraries, with no shell or package manager, to cut size and attack surface.
A tool and YAML specification for defining and running multi-container applications on a single Docker host.
An action packaged as a container image or Dockerfile that runs in its own container, on Linux runners only.
The dockerd daemon and docker CLI that build images and run containers by delegating to containerd and runc.
A text build recipe of instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, USER, ENTRYPOINT and so on) that a builder executes to produce an image.
DORA's software delivery metrics, now five: throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate).
The API (GA in v1.34) for requesting devices such as GPUs through ResourceClaims and DeviceClasses with CEL-based selection, going beyond simple device-plugin counts.
Automatic creation of a PersistentVolume by a StorageClass provisioner when a claim is made, rather than using pre-created static volumes.
A Linux kernel technology that runs verified, sandboxed programs at kernel hook points, powering high-performance networking, observability and security tools.
A Pod-lifetime scratch volume on node disk or memory, shared by the Pod's containers and deleted with the Pod.
The scalable API listing the endpoints (addresses, ports, readiness, zone) behind a Service, replacing the legacy Endpoints API (deprecated in v1.33).
A temporary container added to a running Pod with kubectl debug for troubleshooting, especially distroless images that lack a shell.
A distributed, strongly consistent key-value store using the Raft protocol that holds all Kubernetes cluster state and must be backed up and protected.
A point-in-time backup of the etcd keyspace, taken with etcdctl and restored with etcdutl, which is the core of control-plane disaster recovery.
A CNCF graduated runtime security engine that applies rules to kernel system calls (via eBPF) and Kubernetes audit events to detect suspicious behaviour.
A test that passes and fails on unchanged code, eroding trust in the pipeline; tracked and quarantined through pipeline-health metrics.
A lightweight log and telemetry processor and forwarder from the CNCF-graduated Fluentd project, typically run as a node DaemonSet.
A CNCF graduated GitOps toolkit of composable controllers (source, kustomize, helm, notification, image automation) that reconcile clusters from Git or OCI artifacts.
A server-side copy of a repository under another owner, used to propose changes without write access to the original.
A layered model (Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code) in which each inner layer depends on the security of the layers around it.
Google SRE's recommended user-facing monitoring set: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

Scheduling a group of Pods all-or-nothing so distributed jobs do not deadlock on partial placement. In-tree it uses the Workload/PodGroup API (scheduling.k8s.io/v1beta1, behind the GenericWorkload gate, beta and off by default in v1.37); Kueue and Volcano also provide it.

The role-oriented successor to Ingress: CRDs (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute and others) that split L4/L7 routing duties between infrastructure providers, cluster operators and app developers; HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute are standard-channel, TCPRoute/UDPRoute experimental, and mesh support comes through GAMMA.
A cluster-scoped Gateway API resource naming the controller that implements Gateways of that class (the infrastructure-provider role).
A distributed version control system storing history as a graph of content-addressed commits, trees and blobs, with lightweight branches.
A movable named pointer to a commit that lets lines of work proceed in parallel and later merge.
Git Large File Storage, an extension that replaces large binaries with pointer files and stores their content on an LFS server.
A named reference to a specific commit, lightweight or annotated (optionally signed), used to mark releases.
A branching model with long-lived main and develop branches plus feature, release and hotfix branches, suited to versioned releases but slower to integrate.
Keyed storage (actions/cache or setup-* caching) that reuses dependencies across runs and is evicted by size and age.
The concurrency key that serializes or cancels in-progress runs or jobs sharing a group name, used to prevent overlapping deployments and save minutes.
The strategy.matrix expansion of one job over variables such as OS and runtime versions, with include/exclude, fail-fast and max-parallel controls.

The machine or container that executes workflow jobs, either GitHub-hosted (standard or larger, freshly provisioned per job) or self-hosted (including autoscaled on Kubernetes with Actions Runner Controller).
A Docker container (database, cache, broker) attached to a job through services: for integration tests, with ports and health-check options.
A YAML file in .github/workflows that defines event triggers and jobs of steps that GitHub runs on hosted or self-hosted runners.
Specially formatted log lines and environment files (GITHUB_OUTPUT, GITHUB_ENV, GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY) that steps use to set outputs, mask values, group logs and annotate.

GitHub's application security umbrella for two paid products sold since April 2025, GitHub Secret Protection and GitHub Code Security (both also available for Azure DevOps), alongside the dependency graph and Dependabot alerts that are free on all plans.
GitHub's curated database of security advisories (GHSA IDs cross-referenced to CVEs) for open-source ecosystems, which powers Dependabot alerts.
A first-class GitHub integration identity with fine-grained permissions, installed on organizations or repositories, that authenticates with short-lived installation tokens.

Signed GitHub attestations, created in Actions with Sigstore, that link an artifact's digest to the workflow, repository and commit that built it, so deployments can verify provenance with gh attestation verify or admission policy.

The paid GitHub Advanced Security product (since April 2025) bundling code scanning, the CodeQL CLI, Copilot Autofix, AI Scan, security campaigns, Dependabot auto-triage rules, dependency review and security overview.
Cloud-hosted development environments that run a dev container on GitHub-managed VMs, opened in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs or the browser.

GitHub's AI coding assistant across IDEs, GitHub.com and the terminal, offering inline suggestions, chat, agent mode, the Copilot CLI, code review and Copilot cloud agent under individual (Free, Student, Pro, Pro+, Max) and organization (Business, Enterprise) plans metered in GitHub AI Credits.
A forum-style space in a repository or organization for Q&A, announcements and ideas, outside the issue tracker.
The top-level GitHub Enterprise account that centrally governs policies, billing, identity and audit for many organizations.
A GitHub Enterprise Cloud model where the identity provider creates and controls user accounts, which cannot act outside the enterprise.
The self-hosted GitHub Enterprise appliance, whose features and release cadence lag GitHub Enterprise Cloud (for example, it has no immutable OIDC subject claims).
A lightweight workflow in which work happens on short-lived branches merged to main through reviewed pull requests, with main always deployable.
GitHub releases whose Git tag and assets are locked after publication (the tag cannot move, and its name cannot be reused after deletion); each automatically gets a verifiable release attestation.
GitHub's work-item tracker with labels, milestones, assignees, templates, sub-issues and links to pull requests.
GitHub's catalogue of Actions and Apps, with verified-creator badges, from which workflows consume third-party actions.
A shared GitHub account for teams, with repositories, members, teams, roles and policies, optionally under an enterprise account.
A person who is not an organization member but has been granted access to specific repositories.
GitHub's static-site hosting from a branch or an Actions workflow, often used for documentation sites such as this MkDocs library.
GitHub's planning tool with table, board and roadmap views over issues and pull requests, custom fields, built-in workflows and insights charts.
Named, layerable GitHub rules for branches, tags and pushes, defined at repository, organization or enterprise level, with bypass lists and an evaluate mode.

The paid GitHub Advanced Security product (since April 2025) bundling secret scanning, push protection, AI-detected secrets, custom patterns, delegated bypass, security campaigns and security overview.
A maintainer workflow for privately discussing, fixing and publishing a vulnerability, optionally requesting a CVE, fed by private vulnerability reporting.
A time-boxed, tracked effort to remediate a chosen set of alerts across repositories, assigned to developers and assisted by Copilot Autofix.
A named, reusable set of GitHub security settings (the GitHub-recommended set or custom) applied to many repositories, with defaults for new repositories.
An organization role that grants read access to all repositories and lets holders manage security alerts and settings without admin rights.
Organization- and enterprise-level dashboards of security feature coverage, alert risk and remediation metrics.
A Copilot-powered natural-language builder for small full-stack apps, in public preview for Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise.
An installation access token minted automatically for each workflow job, scoped to the repository by the permissions key and expiring when the job ends.

A workflow file, either public or provided by the organization from the workflow-templates directory of its .github repository, copied into a repository as a starting point and independent of the template once created.

Operating systems from declarative desired state that is versioned and immutable, held in Git or another versioned store such as an OCI registry, which in-cluster agents pull and continuously reconcile, correcting drift.
An opinionated, supported, end-to-end way to build and run a type of service, such as a template, pipeline and runtime, that teams can adopt instead of assembling their own.
Grafana Labs' open-source visualization and alerting front end for Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and many other data sources.
A log aggregation system that indexes only labels and stores compressed log chunks in object storage, queried with LogQL.
Google's user-space application kernel (runsc) that intercepts container system calls to isolate untrusted workloads from the host kernel.
A CNCF-graduated open-source registry with projects, RBAC, replication, vulnerability scanning, signature policies and proxy caching.
HashiCorp's managed service for remote Terraform runs, state, private registry, policy enforcement, run tasks and team governance, connected through the cloud block.
HCP Terraform's per-run OIDC workload identity tokens, exchanged for short-lived Azure, AWS, Google Cloud, Kubernetes or Vault credentials.
A container grouping HCP Terraform workspaces and Stacks for shared permissions and variable sets.
An integration that sends run data to an external service (scanner, cost or policy tool) at pre-plan, post-plan, pre-apply or post-apply and can block the run.
A reusable group of Terraform and environment variables applied to many workspaces or projects.
A Service with clusterIP None that allocates no virtual IP and returns individual Pod DNS records, as used for StatefulSet stable identities.

An endpoint or command reporting whether an application can function (liveness, readiness, dependency status), consumed by orchestrators and load balancers; ASP.NET Core exposes it through MapHealthChecks.

The Kubernetes package manager (now Helm 4) that renders templated charts with values into manifests, applies them with server-side apply, and tracks each installation as a versioned, rollback-capable release.

A controller that changes a workload's replica count from resource, custom or external metrics; configurable tolerance is GA in v1.37, and scale-to-zero for object and external metrics is beta and on by default in v1.37.
A volume mounting a path from the node's filesystem into a Pod; a common escape and privilege-escalation vector that the Baseline Pod Security Standard forbids.
The Gateway API route kind that matches HTTP requests by host, path, header or query, then forwards, splits, mirrors or rewrites them to backends; it attaches to Gateways through parentRefs.

The content-addressable, algorithm-prefixed hash (typically sha256) of an OCI manifest or image index, which immutably identifies exact content, unlike a mutable tag; multi-arch images are pinned by the index digest.
A docker-registry Secret referenced by a Pod or ServiceAccount to authenticate image pulls from a private registry.
A mutable, human-readable reference in a repository (for example :8.0 or :latest) that can be repointed to a different manifest at any time.
A volume that mounts an OCI image or artifact read-only into a Pod (GA in v1.36), useful for shipping models or data as OCI artifacts.
Running containers whose filesystem and binaries cannot change at runtime (readOnlyRootFilesystem, no shell or package manager, no exec), so drift signals compromise.
An operating model where servers and containers are never modified after deployment; changes ship as newly built instances that replace the old ones.
Changing a running container's CPU and memory requests and limits through the Pod resize subresource without recreating it (GA in v1.35).
The single person who coordinates an incident response, delegating operations and communications roles and owning decisions until resolution or handoff.
A classification such as SEV1 to SEV4, based on user, data or business impact, that sets response urgency, roles and communication cadence.
Defining infrastructure in version-controlled, machine-readable files that tools apply repeatably, giving infrastructure changes review, diff, test and rollback like code.
A separately installed proxy and controller (HAProxy, Traefik, Contour, cloud load-balancer controllers) that implements Ingress resources; the community Ingress NGINX controller is retired.
A container that must run to completion before a Pod's app containers start, used for setup such as migrations, waiting on dependencies or fetching config.
Applying open-source collaboration practices (open repositories, pull-request contributions, trusted committers) inside an organization.
The integrated set of tools, APIs, templates and infrastructure a platform team provides for self-service delivery, often surfaced through a developer portal.
A CNCF-graduated service mesh providing mTLS workload identity, traffic management and telemetry, in sidecar mode or sidecarless ambient mode (ztunnel plus waypoint proxies).
A CNCF-graduated distributed-tracing backend and UI, whose v2 is built on the OpenTelemetry Collector.
An action whose action.yml runs Node.js code directly on the runner using a supported Node runtime; fast and cross-platform.
A long-standing open-source, plugin-based automation server (a CD Foundation project) commonly self-hosted for CI/CD.
A lightweight, single-binary, CNCF Sandbox Kubernetes distribution for edge, IoT and labs, with an embedded SQLite or etcd datastore.
A Kubernetes SIG Autoscaling project that launches right-sized nodes directly from pending Pod requirements via NodePools, rather than scaling fixed node groups.
An OCI-compatible runtime that runs each Pod inside a lightweight virtual machine with its own guest kernel, selected through RuntimeClass.
A CNCF graduated project that scales workloads, including to zero, on event sources such as queues and streams by feeding external metrics to the HPA.
The design-document process through which Kubernetes features are proposed, owned by a SIG and tracked through alpha, beta and GA.
Kubernetes IN Docker, a tool that runs conformant single- or multi-node clusters as Docker containers for local testing and CI.
A CNCF-graduated platform for serverless workloads on Kubernetes: request-driven autoscaling with scale-to-zero (Serving) and CloudEvents routing (Eventing).
The control-plane front end that authenticates, authorizes, admits, validates and persists every API request, and the only component that talks to etcd directly.
The control-plane binary running the built-in controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount token and others).

A per-node component that implements Service virtual IPs by programming iptables (the default) or nftables (GA v1.33) rules; IPVS mode is deprecated since v1.35, and v1.37 adds the KubeProxyIPVS gate ahead of its deactivation and removal. Some eBPF CNIs replace kube-proxy entirely.
The control-plane component that binds unscheduled Pods to nodes by filtering and scoring them against requests, affinity, taints, topology and priority.
An exporter that turns Kubernetes object state (Deployments, Pods, Nodes and so on) into Prometheus metrics, as opposed to resource-usage metrics.
The upstream tool that bootstraps and upgrades conformant clusters from a kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4 configuration by generating certificates, static Pod manifests for the control plane, and join tokens.
The client file of clusters, users (certificates, tokens or exec credential plugins) and contexts that kubectl and client libraries use to reach API servers.
The Kubernetes command-line client for declarative and imperative API operations, debugging and plugins.
The node agent that registers the node, keeps the containers described in its Pods running and healthy through the CRI, and reports status to the API server.
An open-source (StackRox/Red Hat) static analysis linter that checks Kubernetes YAML and Helm charts against security and production-readiness rules.
The open-source, CNCF-graduated container orchestration system that continuously reconciles declared desired state for workloads, networking and storage across a cluster of nodes.
The rules for how long deprecated beta and GA API versions must still be served before removal, which force manifest migrations at upgrade time.
The API server's chronological record of requests, filtered by an audit policy into None, Metadata, Request or RequestResponse levels, used for forensics and detection.
The CNCF program certifying that a distribution or managed service passes the upstream conformance tests, keeping workloads portable; it now includes an AI conformance program.
The components (kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, cloud-controller-manager) that store desired cluster state and drive the cluster toward it.
A control loop that watches resources through the API server and keeps acting to make actual state match the declared desired state.
The certificates.k8s.io API through which clients and kubelets request X.509 certificates that a signer issues after approval.
A controller that manages ReplicaSets of interchangeable stateless Pods and provides declarative rolling updates and rollbacks.
API server configuration that encrypts chosen resources such as Secrets before they are written to etcd, ideally through a KMS v2 plugin backed by a cloud key service.
A short-lived API object (one hour by default) recording state changes and warnings such as scheduling failures, image pulls and probe failures.
A key on an object that blocks deletion until a controller finishes cleanup and removes it; a common cause of resources stuck in Terminating.

A frozen Kubernetes API for host- and path-based HTTP(S) routing to Services, implemented by a separately installed Ingress controller; the community Ingress NGINX controller has had no releases or security fixes since March 2026.
A controller that runs Pods until a set number complete successfully, with retry, backoff and parallelism controls.
Sharing clusters among teams or customers with isolation layered from namespaces, RBAC, quotas and policies (soft) up to virtual or dedicated clusters (hard).
A named scope for API objects that provides name isolation and an attachment point for RBAC, quotas and policies, but is not a hard security boundary on its own.
A worker machine (VM or physical) running the kubelet, a container runtime and kube-proxy (or an eBPF replacement) onto which Pods are scheduled.
The certificate authorities (cluster, front-proxy, etcd) and certificates that authenticate control-plane, kubelet and client communication.
The authorization mode that grants verbs on resources through namespaced Roles or cluster-wide ClusterRoles, attached by RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings to users, groups or ServiceAccounts.
An API object for small confidential values that is only base64-encoded by default, so its protection depends on RBAC, encryption at rest and external secret stores.
A stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to a label-selected set of Pods, exposed as ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, ExternalName or headless.
A namespaced Kubernetes identity for workloads that receives short-lived, audience-bound projected tokens and can be federated to cloud identities.
A Special Interest Group that owns an area of Kubernetes (SIG Network, SIG Auth, SIG Node and others) and its subprojects, KEPs and code.
A Pod option (hostUsers: false), stable since Kubernetes v1.36, that maps container root to an unprivileged host UID range to contain breakouts.
The supported version gaps between components (kubelet and kube-proxy up to three minors older than kube-apiserver, kubectl within one minor), which constrain upgrade order.
A CNCF-incubating Kubernetes security platform that scans clusters, manifests and images against frameworks such as NSA/CISA, CIS and MITRE.
ControlPlane's static risk-scoring tool for Kubernetes manifests.
A Kubernetes SIG Scheduling job-queueing controller that admits batch and AI jobs against quotas, with fair sharing, preemption and all-or-nothing admission.
A template-free tool built into kubectl that customizes plain manifests through bases, overlays, patches and components.
A CNCF graduated, Kubernetes-native policy engine whose YAML and CEL policies validate, mutate and generate resources and verify image signatures.
Key-value metadata on objects, plus the equality- or set-based queries that Services, controllers, NetworkPolicies and scheduling rules use to select them.
The elapsed time from a request entering the system to its delivery, spanning queue time plus cycle time.
A namespaced policy that injects default requests and limits and enforces minimum and maximum values per container or Pod at admission.
Kernel-defined subdivisions of root privilege (for example CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_ADMIN) that securityContext can drop or add per container.
Kernel features that give a process its own isolated view of process IDs, network, mounts, hostname and users, forming the isolation half of a container.
A periodic kubelet check that restarts a container when it fails, meant to recover from deadlocks rather than to signal temporary unavailability.
Exercising a system at expected peak load to verify latency and throughput; distinct from stress (beyond limits), soak (long duration) and spike (sudden surge) tests.
Linux containers that boot an init system and run several services like a lightweight VM, unlike single-process application containers.
How a pull request lands: merge commit, squash, rebase, or semi-linear merge in Azure Repos, trading history fidelity against linearity.
A text-based diagram syntax rendered in GitHub and Azure DevOps Markdown and wikis for flowcharts, sequence diagrams and Gantt charts.
A numeric time series identified by a name and labels and typed as a counter, gauge or histogram.
The number of unique label-value combinations for a metric, which drives storage and query cost and explodes when unbounded values like user IDs become labels.
The add-on that scrapes kubelet resource metrics and serves the Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io, v1 since Kubernetes v1.37) used by kubectl top and the HPA.
Collecting and alerting on predefined metrics and checks to detect known failure modes, in contrast to observability's open-ended investigation.
A single repository holding many projects with shared tooling and atomic cross-project changes, in contrast to one repository per service (polyrepo).
An average time-to-restore metric whose R variously means repair, recovery, respond or resolve; DORA replaced it with failed deployment recovery time.
A Dockerfile technique that keeps compilers and build tooling in earlier stages and copies only runtime artifacts into a small final image.
Servers updated in place over their lifetime (patches, configuration pushes), which invites drift and snowflake servers.
An in-process CEL-based admission policy, stable since Kubernetes v1.36, that mutates objects through apply configurations or JSON Patch without a webhook.
An init container with restartPolicy Always (GA in v1.33) that starts before the app containers, keeps running beside them and stops after them.
A namespaced L3/L4 allow-list for Pod ingress and egress selected by labels, namespaces or IP blocks, enforced only if the CNI plugin supports it.
Pod-side required or preferred scheduling rules that attract Pods to nodes with matching labels, a richer form of nodeSelector.
Cordoning a node to stop new scheduling, then evicting its Pods while honouring PodDisruptionBudgets, before maintenance or an upgrade.
The authorization mode and admission plugin that limit each kubelet to reading and modifying only objects tied to its own node and Pods.
The ability to explain a system's internal state, including novel failures, from its external telemetry (logs, metrics, traces and profiles).
Non-image content (signatures, SBOMs, attestations, Helm charts, models) stored in an OCI registry; the OCI 1.1 subject field and referrers API link it to the image it describes.
An OCI manifest listing platform-specific image manifests, so one tag or digest resolves to the right image per OS and architecture.
Open Container Initiative standards for the image format, the registry distribution API and the runtime bundle, so images built by any tool run on any compliant runtime.
The rotation of engineers who must respond to pages within an agreed time, with escalation policies, handoffs and load limits.
An admission controller that enforces Open Policy Agent Rego policies through ConstraintTemplate and Constraint CRDs and audits existing resources.
A CNCF-incubating project and specification for real-time Kubernetes cost allocation by namespace, workload and label.
A CNCF-incubating, vendor-neutral feature-flag API and SDK specification, with .NET and Python SDKs, that decouples flag evaluation from the flag provider.
An open YAML specification for declaring SLIs, SLOs and alerting policies in a vendor-neutral way.
The CNCF graduated, vendor-neutral standard of APIs, SDKs, semantic conventions, the OTLP protocol and the Collector for generating and exporting traces, metrics and logs.
A vendor-neutral telemetry pipeline that receives, processes (batching, filtering, sampling, enrichment) and exports telemetry, deployed as a per-node agent or a central gateway.
The language implementation of the OpenTelemetry API that samples, processes and exports telemetry; libraries depend only on the API, while applications configure the SDK.

The MPL-2.0 fork of Terraform, a CNCF Sandbox project (Linux Foundation) since April 2025, with a compatible language and provider protocol plus its own features such as client-side state encryption and OCI registry support.
Encoding operational knowledge for an application in a custom controller that reconciles CRDs to automate install, upgrade, backup and failover.
OpenTelemetry's standard attribute names and values (for example service.name, http.request.method) that make telemetry comparable across languages and vendors.
OpenTelemetry's gRPC/HTTP protocol for sending traces, metrics and logs (stable for all three) from SDKs to Collectors and backends.
A hosted package repository (NuGet, npm, PyPI, Maven) with views or promotion levels and upstream sources that proxy public registries.
HashiCorp's tool for building identical machine and container images for many platforms from one HCL template using builders and provisioners.
A cluster-scoped piece of storage, provisioned statically or dynamically through a StorageClass, with a lifecycle independent of any Pod.
A namespaced request for storage of a given size, access mode and class that binds to a PersistentVolume and is mounted by Pods.
A user-scoped token used instead of a password for Git, API and CLI access; GitHub offers fine-grained and classic PATs, and Azure DevOps offers scoped PATs.
Running an internal platform with product-management practices: user research, a roadmap, adoption and satisfaction metrics, and voluntary use.
The discipline of building and running internal platforms as products that give development teams self-service, paved paths to build, deploy and operate software.
The smallest deployable Kubernetes unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace, IP address and volumes, scheduled together onto one node.
Scheduling rules that place Pods near or away from other Pods with matching labels within a topology domain such as a node or zone.
The PodCertificateRequest API and podCertificate projected-volume source (GA in v1.37) that issue X.509 workload certificates to Pods for mTLS identity.
A policy that limits how many Pods of a workload voluntary disruptions (drains, upgrades, autoscaler consolidation) may evict at once.
The built-in admission controller that applies a Pod Security Standard per namespace through enforce, audit and warn labels.
The former cluster-level Pod security admission API, removed in Kubernetes v1.25 and replaced by Pod Security Admission and policy engines.
Three cumulative profiles, Privileged, Baseline and Restricted, that define which Pod security settings are allowed; they replaced PodSecurityPolicy.
A daemonless container engine with a Docker-compatible CLI that runs containers and pods rootless or rootful without a central daemon.
Expressing governance and security rules as version-controlled, testable code that tools evaluate automatically against IaC plans, manifests or live resources.
A cluster object assigning Pods a scheduling priority, which drives preemption of lower-priority Pods.
A checklist assessment of a service's reliability, observability, capacity and operability before launch or SRE handover.
Releasing to progressively larger audiences (rings, canaries, flags) with automated metric analysis gating each step and automatic rollback.
One volume that combines Secrets, ConfigMaps, downward API data, bound service account tokens and ClusterTrustBundles in a single directory.
A CNCF graduated monitoring system that scrapes metrics from targets into a time-series database, queries them with PromQL and evaluates alerting rules.
A process that exposes metrics on a /metrics endpoint for a system without native Prometheus support (node_exporter, blackbox_exporter, database exporters).
An operator that manages Prometheus and Alertmanager through CRDs such as ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor and PrometheusRule; the core of kube-prometheus-stack.
A Prometheus rule that precomputes a PromQL expression into a new series, for fast dashboards and SLO burn-rate calculations.
The protocol Prometheus and agents use to push samples to remote, long-term or managed metric stores.
Prometheus's functional query language for selecting, aggregating and computing rates over time series, also used by managed Prometheus services.
A proposal to merge one branch into another, with review, discussion, status checks and a merge strategy; GitHub and Azure Repos both use the term.
An IaC platform that defines infrastructure in general-purpose languages (C#, Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, YAML), with a state backend and a preview/up workflow.
A pipeline that holds target credentials and applies changes to environments from outside, as opposed to in-cluster agents pulling desired state.
A Secret Protection feature that blocks pushes containing detected secrets before they enter the repository, with audited bypass reasons or delegated bypass approval.
The PersistentVolume capabilities ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany and ReadWriteOncePod, which limit how many nodes or Pods may mount a volume.
Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort, derived from a Pod's requests and limits, which sets eviction order under node memory pressure.
An automated or manual checkpoint (tests, coverage, scans, approvals) that a change must pass to advance to the next stage.
A periodic check that, while failing, removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it, so traffic only reaches instances able to serve.
Collecting performance and error data from real user sessions in browsers or apps (Core Web Vitals, JavaScript errors).
What happens to a PersistentVolume's backing storage when its claim is released: Retain or Delete (Recycle is deprecated).
A service-monitoring heuristic tracking request Rate, Errors and Duration for every service.
A controller that keeps a set number of identical Pod replicas running, normally owned by a Deployment rather than used directly.
A namespace-level object that caps aggregate resource consumption and object counts, unlike a LimitRange, which sets per-container defaults and bounds.
Per-container CPU and memory settings where requests reserve capacity for scheduling and limits cap usage, with CPU overuse throttled and memory overuse OOM-killed.
A workflow triggered by workflow_call that other workflows invoke as a job, with typed inputs, secrets and outputs, centralizing versioned pipeline logic.
Releasing to successively larger predefined audiences (internal, early adopters, broad) with gates between rings.
The default Deployment strategy, which replaces Pods incrementally within maxSurge and maxUnavailable and keeps revision history for kubectl rollout undo.
Investigating why an incident happened; current practice favours multiple contributing factors over a single root cause.
Running the container engine and runtime themselves as an unprivileged user (rootless Docker or Podman), unlike Kubernetes user namespaces, which remap the container's root.
A documented, ideally automatable, step-by-step procedure for diagnosing and mitigating a known alert or operational task.
The OCI reference low-level runtime that creates a container from an OCI bundle using namespaces, cgroups and seccomp.
An organization- or enterprise-level collection of runners with access policies controlling which repositories and workflows may use them.
An API object that selects a container runtime handler per Pod, used to run untrusted workloads in sandboxes such as gVisor or Kata Containers.
The OASIS Static Analysis Results Interchange Format, a JSON format that static analyzers emit and code scanning ingests.
A Git-bundled tool that tunes large repositories with partial clone, sparse checkout, background maintenance and the filesystem monitor.
Docker's empty base (FROM scratch) for statically linked binaries; smaller than distroless because it has no libc, CA bundle or time-zone data.
An attack where attacker-controlled event data, such as a PR title or branch name, is interpolated via an expression into a run script and executed with the workflow's privileges.
The phases (plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor) and models (waterfall, iterative, agile) by which software moves from idea to production.
A Linux kernel facility that filters which system calls a process may make, applied in Kubernetes through securityContext profiles such as RuntimeDefault.
Detecting credentials committed to repositories, including their history, by matching provider and custom patterns; it raises alerts and, for partner patterns, notifies the issuer.
A Secret Protection check that asks the issuing provider whether a detected secret is still active, so that live leaks are fixed first.
Pod- and container-level settings that control user and group IDs, privilege escalation, Linux capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux and read-only root filesystems.
A label-based mandatory access control LSM applied to Pods through seLinuxOptions and enforced by default on RHEL and OpenShift nodes.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering in which a major bump signals breaking changes, minor adds compatible features and patch fixes bugs.
HashiCorp's proprietary policy-as-code language enforced in HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise workspace runs (not Stacks) at advisory, soft-mandatory or hard-mandatory levels.
API-server-side merging of declarative configuration with per-field ownership (managedFields) that detects conflicts between managers such as Helm, GitOps controllers and kubectl.
An infrastructure layer of proxies (sidecar, per-node or ambient) that provides workload identity, mTLS, traffic management and telemetry for service-to-service calls.
A discipline that applies software engineering to operations, managing reliability through SLOs, error budgets, toil reduction and blameless learning.
A developer-productivity model spanning Satisfaction and well-being, Performance, Activity, Communication and collaboration, and Efficiency and flow.
A named, timed operation within a trace, with attributes, events, status and parent-child links.
A probe that holds off liveness and readiness checks until a slow-starting container reports it has started, preventing premature restarts.
A controller for Pods that need stable network identities, ordered rollout and per-replica persistent volumes, such as databases and message brokers.
A Pod the kubelet runs directly from a manifest directory (for example /etc/kubernetes/manifests); this is how kubeadm runs control-plane components.
A cluster object naming a CSI provisioner, its parameters, reclaim policy and volume binding mode, used to create PersistentVolumes on demand.
Emitting logs as machine-parseable events with consistent named fields and trace correlation (ILogger message templates, Serilog, Python structlog).
Scripted probes (availability pings, multi-step browser journeys) run on a schedule from external locations to catch failures before users do.
A node-side repel mechanism: a taint keeps Pods off a node unless they carry a matching toleration, which permits but does not force placement there.
A CNCF-incubating, Kubernetes-native CI/CD framework of Task and Pipeline CRDs that run steps in Pods.
HashiCorp's (an IBM company) declarative, provider-based IaC tool that plans and applies HCL configurations against any API with a provider, tracking resources in state.

The configured storage for CLI state, such as local, azurerm, s3, gcs and other backends, which decides where state lives and how concurrent runs are locked; HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise are connected with the cloud block instead.
The terraform cloud configuration block that connects a working directory to HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise workspaces, replacing the legacy remote backend.
Variable validation, resource preconditions and postconditions, and check blocks that assert assumptions and fail or warn during plan and apply.
A data block that reads existing infrastructure or computed values for use in configuration without managing their lifecycle.
The .terraform.lock.hcl file recording the exact provider versions and checksums chosen by terraform init, committed for reproducible runs.
The self-hosted distribution of the HCP Terraform platform, for organizations that must run it in their own environment.
A Terraform construct (v1.10+) whose values exist only during a run and are never written to plan or state, used for secrets and short-lived credentials.

A configuration block that brings existing infrastructure under Terraform management during plan and apply, optionally generating configuration; it replaces the imperative terraform import command, which edits state outside a plan.
A typed, optionally validated and sensitive module parameter set through tfvars files, -var, TF_VAR_ environment variables or HCP variable sets.
The arguments every resource or module block accepts (count, for_each, depends_on, provider and lifecycle), which control how many instances exist, their ordering and replacement.
A reusable, versioned directory of Terraform configuration with input variables and outputs, called from other configurations and sourced from local paths, Git or registries.
A refactoring declaration mapping an old resource or module address to a new one, so Terraform updates state instead of destroying and recreating.
A value a module exports to its caller, the CLI or remote-state consumers, optionally sensitive or ephemeral.
Terraform's computed set of create, update, replace and destroy actions from configuration, state and refreshed reality; it can be saved for an exact apply.

HashiCorp's native HCL-based policy-as-code framework. It is GA in the Terraform CLI from v1.17.0 (2026-10-21, via -policies) and documented as beta in HCP Terraform, where it applies to workspaces and Stacks.
A plugin that maps Terraform resource and data types to a platform's API, versioned and installed from a registry during terraform init.
An additional named configuration of the same provider (for example a second region or subscription), selected per resource or passed into modules.
A plan mode (-refresh-only) that updates state to match real infrastructure without proposing configuration changes, used to review drift.
HashiCorp's public registry of providers and modules that terraform init downloads from; HCP Terraform's private registry is the internal counterpart.
A declaration (v1.7+) that removes a resource from Terraform management, optionally without destroying it (lifecycle destroy = false).
A variable, output or attribute that Terraform redacts in CLI output but still stores in plain text in state.
An HCP Terraform configuration layer (GA) that composes modules as components and deploys them repeatedly as isolated deployments, such as per environment or region; beyond the TF-A 004 objectives.
The JSON record mapping configuration addresses to real resource IDs and attributes, which Terraform uses to plan changes and which can contain secrets.
The backend mechanism (blob lease, S3 lockfile, HCP Terraform run queue) that prevents concurrent operations from writing the same state.
Terraform's built-in test framework, using .tftest.hcl files with run blocks, assertions and mock providers, for modules and configurations.
In the CLI, an additional named state for the same configuration; in HCP Terraform, a full unit of runs with its own state, variables, permissions and VCS settings.
A resource argument (v1.11+) that accepts ephemeral values such as passwords and is never persisted in plan or state.
The guideline of many fast unit tests, fewer integration or service tests and few end-to-end UI tests, each run at the earliest, cheapest stage.
A Cilium sub-project for eBPF-based runtime security observability that can also enforce policy in-kernel, for example by killing a process on a match.
A CNCF-incubating project that adds global querying, deduplication and object-storage long-term retention to Prometheus.
An alert that fires when a metric crosses a static value for a duration; simple, but noisier than SLO burn-rate alerts.
Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales with service size and produces no lasting value, which SRE teams cap and engineer away.
Pod rules that bound how unevenly matching Pods may be spread across zones, nodes or other topology keys.
Choosing which traces to keep, either up front by probability (head-based) or after completion by errors or latency (tail-based, in the Collector).
Aqua Security's open-source scanner for vulnerabilities, IaC and Kubernetes misconfigurations, secrets and licences, which also generates SBOMs.
A branching model where developers integrate small changes into the main branch at least daily, using short-lived branches and feature flags instead of long-lived branches.
Brendan Gregg's resource heuristic of checking Utilization, Saturation and Errors for every resource (CPU, memory, disk, network).
An in-process admission policy (GA in v1.30) written as CEL expressions that validates requests without running a webhook server.
An open-source (vmware-tanzu) tool that backs up and restores Kubernetes resources and persistent volumes to object storage and migrates workloads between clusters.
An add-on that recommends or applies CPU and memory requests from observed usage, resizing Pods instead of adding replicas; its in-place update mode builds on in-place pod resize (GA v1.35).
A CSI-backed point-in-time copy of a PersistentVolumeClaim, defined through a VolumeSnapshotClass and used for backup and cloning.
A W3C header that propagates application key-value context across service calls, separately from trace and span identifiers.
The W3C standard traceparent and tracestate HTTP headers that carry trace and span IDs between services so traces join across vendors.
Containers that share a Windows Server kernel (process isolation) or run in a utility VM (Hyper-V isolation), built from Server Core or Nano Server bases.
Files a job uploads to keep outputs for download or for later jobs, subject to retention policies.
OpenTelemetry instrumentation added without code changes, through agents, bytecode manipulation, monkey patching or eBPF, for .NET, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP and Python.

pairs.difference: A failing liveness probe restarts the container; a failing readiness probe only removes the Pod from Service endpoints until it recovers.
Deployment replicas are interchangeable and share storage semantics; StatefulSet replicas keep stable names, ordered rollout and their own PersistentVolumeClaims.
Both are consumed the same way, but Secrets get tighter RBAC, tmpfs mounts and optional encryption at rest; base64 encoding itself protects nothing.
Requests drive scheduling and guaranteed share; limits cap usage, with CPU overuse throttled and memory overuse OOM-killed.
Taints let nodes repel Pods, while affinity lets Pods seek nodes; a toleration permits placement but never attracts a Pod.

Ingress is a single frozen HTTP resource extended by controller-specific annotations; Gateway API splits roles across typed CRDs, with HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute in the standard channel, TCPRoute/UDPRoute still experimental, and mesh traffic handled through GAMMA.
NetworkPolicy filters L3/L4 traffic by labels and IPs in the CNI; mesh policies authorize L7 requests by cryptographic workload identity.
A Role grants permissions in one namespace; a ClusterRole defines cluster-scoped or reusable permissions whose reach depends on whether a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding uses it.
PSS are the policy definitions (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted); PSA is the built-in admission controller that enforces, audits or warns on them per namespace.
VAP runs CEL in-process with no service to operate; webhooks call external code, which is more flexible but adds latency and an availability dependency.
Kyverno policies are Kubernetes-style YAML/CEL with mutate, generate and verifyImages built in; Gatekeeper uses general-purpose Rego that is also reusable outside Kubernetes.
Helm templates manifests and tracks versioned releases with rollback; Kustomize patches plain YAML with no templates and no release state.
A CRD only adds a new API type and storage; an operator is the controller that gives that type behaviour by reconciling it.
HPA changes the replica count, while VPA changes per-Pod CPU and memory requests; they conflict if both act on the same resource metric.
HPA scales on metrics already exposed through the metrics APIs; KEDA connects external event sources and handles activation from zero, then feeds the HPA.
Cluster Autoscaler resizes predefined node groups; Karpenter provisions individually right-sized nodes from pending Pod requirements and consolidates them.
seccomp filters which system calls a process may make; AppArmor confines which files, capabilities and network resources a program may access.
runc containers share the host kernel directly; sandboxes put a user-space kernel or micro-VM in between, trading performance for isolation.
Tags are mutable pointers that can be retargeted; digests are content hashes that always identify the same bytes, so deploy and sign by digest.
Compose declares containers on one host with no cross-machine self-healing; Kubernetes reconciles desired state across a cluster, at much higher operational cost.

They share HCL and the provider protocol, but Terraform is BSL-licensed by HashiCorp (IBM) with HCP-centric features like Stacks and Terraform Policy, while OpenTofu is MPL-2.0, a CNCF Sandbox project since April 2025, with features such as client-side state encryption.
A CLI workspace is just another state file for the same configuration; an HCP workspace is a full unit with its own variables, permissions, run history and VCS connection.
Sentinel is HashiCorp's proprietary language embedded in HCP Terraform and Enterprise; OPA/Rego is a CNCF general-purpose engine used across Terraform, Kubernetes and APIs.
Continuous delivery keeps every change releasable but leaves a human release decision; continuous deployment ships every passing change automatically.
Blue-green switches all traffic at once between two full environments; canary moves a small, growing share of traffic while comparing metrics.
Reusable workflows are whole jobs invoked with workflow_call, with their own runners, secrets and environments; composite actions bundle steps that run inside the caller's job.
GITHUB_TOKEN is minted per job, scoped to the repository and expires with the job; PATs are long-lived user credentials and a frequent leak source.

Both run YAML CI/CD with environments that carry approvals and scoped secrets. Azure Pipelines adds first-class stages, a broader checks catalogue (business hours, Azure Monitor alerts, invoke REST/Function, exclusive lock, required template), extends templates for governance and native Boards/Artifacts/Test Plans integration; Actions has the larger action ecosystem, GitHub-wide event triggers and reusable workflows.

Both are vendor-managed, scalable build compute, but Managed DevOps Pools serves Azure DevOps agents with custom images and Azure networking billed through your Azure subscription, while larger runners serve GitHub Actions jobs.
Argo CD is an application-centric GitOps server with UI, SSO and ApplicationSets; Flux is a set of composable controllers with no built-in UI that favours Kubernetes-native CRDs.
Push pipelines hold cluster credentials and apply changes once; GitOps agents inside the cluster pull desired state and keep correcting drift.
Trunk-based development integrates small changes into main at least daily behind flags; GitFlow keeps long-lived develop and release branches that delay integration.
Secret Protection detects and blocks leaked credentials (push protection, validity checks); Code Security finds vulnerable code and dependencies (CodeQL, dependency review, Autofix, campaigns).
Dependabot alerts flag vulnerable dependencies already on a branch; dependency review stops a pull request from introducing them before merge.
An SLO is an internal reliability target that sets the error budget; an SLA is a contractual promise with penalties, deliberately looser than the SLO.
cosign favours keyless signing with OIDC identities and a public transparency log; Notation uses X.509 PKI and trust policies, common with registry and key-vault integrations.

Podman is daemonless and runs rootless by default, with each container a child of the calling process; Docker Engine routes every operation through the long-running dockerd daemon, which runs as root unless rootless mode is configured.
containerd is a general-purpose runtime used by Docker, Kubernetes and others; CRI-O implements only the Kubernetes CRI and versions in lockstep with Kubernetes minors.

A Linux namespace is a kernel isolation primitive for a process's view of PIDs, network or mounts; a Kubernetes namespace is only an API scoping unit for names, RBAC and quotas, with no kernel isolation.
cgroups limit how much CPU, memory and I/O a process group can use; namespaces limit what it can see. A container needs both.
An init container runs to completion before app containers start; a native sidecar (restartPolicy Always) starts first but keeps running for the Pod's life and stops after the app containers.
A startup probe only gates the start of a slow container and then hands over; a liveness probe runs for the container's whole life and restarts it on failure.
A Job runs Pods to completion once; a CronJob creates a new Job on each cron schedule tick, with concurrency and history policies.
A PV is cluster-scoped storage supplied by an admin or provisioner; a PVC is a namespaced request that binds to one PV and is what Pods mount.
Static provisioning pre-creates PVs for claims to bind; dynamic provisioning lets a StorageClass's CSI provisioner create a PV when a claim appears.
Retain keeps the backing volume and data after the claim is deleted for manual recovery; Delete removes the backing storage with the PV.
RWO allows read-write mounts from a single node, so several Pods on that node can share it; RWOP restricts the volume to exactly one Pod in the cluster.
NodePort opens a static port on every node for external traffic; LoadBalancer asks the cloud controller to provision an external load balancer that fronts those node ports or Pod IPs.

The Ingress resource is declarative routing configuration; the Ingress controller is the separately installed proxy that reads it and actually serves traffic. Without a controller, Ingress objects do nothing.

NetworkPolicy is a namespaced, allow-only API owned by app teams; ClusterNetworkPolicy is a cluster-scoped, priority-ordered CRD with Admin rules evaluated before and Baseline rules after namespaced policies, and it needs a CNI that implements it.
VAP accepts or rejects requests with CEL expressions; MAP changes objects through apply configurations or JSON Patch. Both run in-process without a webhook.
PSA enforces only the three fixed Pod Security Standards per namespace; Kyverno is an add-on engine for arbitrary validate, mutate, generate and image-verification policies.
A chart is a versioned package of templates and default values; a release is one installed instance of a chart in a cluster, with its own revision history.
apply is declarative and idempotent, merging desired state (client-side or server-side apply); create is imperative and fails if the object already exists.

An etcd snapshot restores the whole control-plane state but not volume data; Velero backs up selected namespaces' resources and persistent volumes to object storage and can restore them into another cluster.
Device plugins advertise hardware as opaque countable resources; DRA lets Pods claim devices through ResourceClaims with CEL selection, sharing and structured parameters.
A sensitive value is only redacted in CLI output and is still stored in plan and state; an ephemeral value is never written to plan or state at all.
The import block is declarative, reviewed in a plan and can generate configuration; the terraform import command writes to state immediately with no plan.
A moved block renames an address so state follows the refactor without destroying anything; a removed block stops managing a resource, optionally leaving it in place.
A CLI-driven run starts from a local terraform plan or apply against an HCP workspace; a VCS-driven run is triggered by commits and pull requests in a connected repository.

Sentinel is a proprietary language that HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise apply to workspace runs only; Terraform Policy is HCL-based, GA in the Terraform CLI from v1.17.0, and covers both workspaces and Stacks in HCP Terraform (where it is documented as beta).

Branch protection is one rule set per branch pattern in one repository; rulesets are named, layerable rules for branches, tags and pushes at repository, organization or enterprise level, with bypass lists and an evaluate mode.

Both require reviews and status checks before merge; Azure Repos policies add linked work items, comment resolution, build validation and per-branch merge-type limits, while GitHub layers rulesets, CODEOWNERS and required deployments.
A merge commit preserves the branch's full history and topology; squash collapses it to one commit, and rebase replays the commits linearly, losing the merge point.
A cache speeds up later runs by restoring dependencies by key and can be evicted at any time; an artifact preserves a run's outputs for download or later jobs under a retention policy.
A repository secret is available to every workflow job in the repository; an environment secret is released only to jobs that target that environment and pass its protection rules.
A workflow template is copied into a repository once and then diverges; a reusable workflow is called at run time through workflow_call, so updates reach every caller.
GitHub-hosted runners are fresh, GitHub-maintained VMs per job billed by the minute; self-hosted runners run on your machines, reach private networks and keep state unless made ephemeral.
ARC autoscales ephemeral GitHub runners as Pods on your Kubernetes cluster; scale set agents autoscale Azure Pipelines agents on an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set you own.
A canary compares a new version's health against the baseline to decide whether to proceed; an A/B test compares variants' business outcomes on randomized cohorts.
A feature flag changes which code path runs per user or cohort and is meant to be removed; a configuration setting tunes how the same code behaves and is long-lived.
Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment with its own Rollout CRD and analysis templates; Flagger keeps the Deployment and drives canaries through a mesh or ingress, integrated with Flux.
RED measures each service's request Rate, Errors and Duration from the caller's view; USE measures each resource's Utilization, Saturation and Errors from the infrastructure view.
Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints on its own schedule and detects down targets; OTLP clients push telemetry to a Collector or backend, which suits short-lived jobs and firewalled sources.
Synthetic monitoring runs scripted probes on a schedule, even with no traffic; RUM records what real users experience, with real devices and networks, but only where users go.
MTTR averages recovery from any failure, with an ambiguous R; DORA's failed deployment recovery time measures only recovery from failures caused by deployments.
Cycle time runs from starting work on an item to finishing it; DORA's change lead time runs from commit to running in production.

SRE incident management restores service quickly and learns blamelessly; security incident response also preserves evidence, contains an adversary and meets disclosure duties, so roles and communications differ.
The platform is the whole set of self-service capabilities, APIs and infrastructure; the portal is one user interface onto it, and a portal without a platform behind it is only a catalogue.
Crossplane reconciles infrastructure continuously from Kubernetes CRDs and composes it into platform APIs; Terraform plans and applies on demand from HCL with state, correcting drift only when run.
Code scanning is GitHub's alerting and triage feature that ingests SARIF from any analyzer; CodeQL is one analysis engine that produces those results.
Security updates open PRs only to fix dependencies with known vulnerabilities; version updates open PRs on a schedule to keep dependencies current, configured in dependabot.yml.
Push protection blocks a secret before it enters the repository; secret scanning alerts report secrets already in the history, which must then be revoked and rotated.
Agent mode works interactively in your IDE on your machine with your approval of each step; the cloud agent works asynchronously in an ephemeral GitHub cloud environment and returns a pull request.
Custom instructions are applied automatically to every relevant request; prompt files are reusable task prompts you invoke on demand.
Content exclusion stops chosen files from being used as Copilot input; the public code filter governs whether output that matches public code is blocked or shown with references.
